 5 K-Dramas that had us hooked on the cast but confused by the plot: When the Stars Gossip to Sisyphus
 The shows had it all, brilliant casts, budget, and then it all implodes 
 Last updated: November 07, 2026 | 07:23 Lakshana N Palat , Assistant Features Editor 4 MIN READ Add as a preferred source on Google A glimpse of When the Stars Gossip Some K-dramas have it all : chaebol-level budgets, dream leads and enough star power to light up Seoul. Then the show arrives. We’ve all been there: pressing play on a drama with a cast so dazzling it should be illegal, only to find ourselves sixteen episodes deep in plot holes, baffling twists and endings that make us want to hurl the remote. 
 From a space romance that never achieved liftoff to a time-travel thriller that lost track of its own timelines, here are five K-dramas where even a dream cast couldn’t save the script. Grab your popcorn and plenty of patience.
 1) Sisyphus: The Myth 
 Cho Seung-woo plays a genius engineer, Park Shin-hye is a soldier sent back from a ruined future, and the premise is a time-travel thriller with the end of the world at stake. It should've been a blockbuster. On screen, the rules of time travel seem to be rewritten whenever the plot backs itself into a corner, villains pop up mainly to keep the chase going, and a lot of the runtime goes to people sprinting through Seoul. Park Shin-hye throws herself into the action, and Cho Seung-woo brings real gravity to a man haunted by his own inventions. But the show is fittingly named. Like the king of myth, it keeps pushing its boulder up the hill, only to watch it roll back down every time logic is needed.
 2) Snowdrop 
 On paper, Snowdrop looked like a sure thing. It came from the writer and director behind SKY Castle , one of the biggest hits in Korean cable history. It paired Jung Hae-in, the nation’s favorite boyfriend, with Blackpink’s Jisoo in her first lead role. And it set them in 1987 Seoul, the year of the democracy uprising, with Cold War intrigue running underneath. The premise had real romantic potential: a sheltered university student finds a bleeding young man in her dormitory, assumes he’s a pro-democracy activist on the run, and hides him. He’s actually a North Korean agent. 
 After a promising start, it locked its characters inside a women’s dormitory for a hostage standoff that stretched on for roughly half the series. Endless corridor negotiations and spy-agency double-crosses crowded out the romance the show was supposedly about. Jung Hae-in smolders on cue, and Jisoo is earnest in every frame, though she was often visibly outmatched by veterans like Yoo In-na and Kim Hye-yoon. But a love story needs room to breathe. Snowdrop spent most of its run holding its breath, hoping no one would notice it had nowhere to go.
 3) Bride of Habaek 
 On paper, Bride of Habaek promised a smug water deity, a skeptical psychiatrist, and a beloved manhwa as source material. The cast was a who’s-who of young stars: Nam Joo-hyuk, Shin Se-kyung, Lim Ju-hwan, Krystal and Gong Myung. Then the drama stripped the god of his powers, moved him to modern Seoul, and left the story with very little current. Fans of the original barely recognised it, and newcomers wondered why a deity’s homecoming felt so much like waiting in line at a bank. Nam Joo-hyuk looks every inch divine, but the script keeps him wandering around like a tourist who lost his luggage. For a show about a water deity, it was surprisingly dry.
 4) Jirisan 
 Jun Ji-hyun and Ju Ji-hoon were cast as park rangers on Korea’s most majestic mountain, Kingdom’s Kim Eun-hee wrote the script, the director of Goblin and Descendants of the Sun was behind the camera, and the budget was enormous. It should have been a summit. Instead, the scenery often looked like a screensaver, sandwich product placement turned up in the least likely places, and a supernatural murder mystery wandered off the trail for weeks at a time. The leads do their best with long, meaningful stares into the mist. But a show set on a mountain shouldn’t feel this much like a slog up one, and Jirisan left plenty of viewers stranded halfway.
 5) When the Stars Gossip 
 When the Stars Gossip was sold as the first K-drama set on a space station, with a budget of roughly 50 billion won. It brought Lee Min-ho back to the small screen opposite Gong Hyo-jin, the reigning queen of romantic comedy. Hyo-jin plays Eve Kim, a by-the-book commander running a zero-gravity station. Min-ho plays Gong Ryong, a gynecologist who boards as a “space tourist” with a secret mission: carry out IVF in orbit so a wealthy family can get the heir it badly wants. 
 In theory, that’s the kind of gloriously unhinged premise K-drama fans love. In practice, the show never decided whether it wanted to be a workplace comedy, a sci-fi thriller, or a fertility melodrama, so it floated between all three. Awkward scenes turned up as early as the first episode, adding confusion rather than heat. Eve’s ex-boyfriend drifted around the station complicating things nobody had asked to be complicated. The two leads, each famous for sparking with their co-stars, somehow canceled each other out, and the big romantic confessions landed with all the warmth of the vacuum outside. 
 Ratings sank below 2 percent, analysts trimmed their forecasts for the studio, and the finale sent off the few remaining loyalists more baffled than moved. The visuals are genuinely stunning, and both stars look like they belong on a movie poster. But this is a love story set in space that never achieves liftoff. Houston, the problem was the script.
